newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico '97 central bank approach to shift - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Mexico '97 central bank approach to shift - analyst.

text.p: The most important change in Mexico's monetary policy for 1997 will be not so much its overall stance as its implementation, J.P. Morgan economist Alfredo Thorne said in a market report.
Banco de Mexico plans to release the detailed version of its 1997 monetary plan later this week, building on the bare bones of the package it released late last year.
Thorne said that the stance of monetary policy will likely remain on hold, with real interest rates averaging about 7.0 to 10.0 percent.

"Encouragingly, now that inflation expectations for 1997 hover around 18 percent, the authorities have a better chance both to meet their 15 percent inflation target and to retain credibility with price and wage setters than they did in 1996 (when the gulf between a 20.5 percent target and market expectations for 35 percent was vastly wider)," he wrote.

While public sector prices and nominal wage hikes will have limited effect on 1997 inflation, he warned of accelerating domestic demand, looser fiscal policy, tighter labor markets and greater exchange rate fluctuations.
A key for the central bank will be to have its monetary policy credibility to influence contractual wage negotiations, he said.
Thorne said monetary policy will now become more willing to accomodate peso moves warranted by the economic fundamentals.
Foreign reserves will also be rebuilt during the year in response to greater capital inflows, which will cause the central bank to over-achieve its net domestic credit target.
But the central bank will leave the monetary base targets unchanged, "lest provision of excess liquidity threatens loss of inflation discipline," he said.
He said the central bank will publish an intended trajectory of estimated base money, which will allow closer market monitoring.

"Meanwhile a trend is underway to use nominal interest rates (given its response to changes in settlement balances targets) as a superior operational (and quasi-intermediate) target that gives more information on market responses and central bank shifts in policy," Thorne said.
